A1.justification: Both PDFs describe STGC and retain matching core formulations and benchmark results. Text, equations, tables and figures are readable throughout. v2 ends after its references; v3 additionally contains supplementary Sections 6.1–6.7.

before.justification: v2 reports original STGC benchmark comparisons, ablations, gradient analyses and expert-loading results in Tables 1–5 and Figures 1, 3 and 4.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds routing comparisons, language-task evaluations, computational measurements and gradient diagnostics, including Tables 8–14.

M1.justification: The central STGC identification procedure and regularizer remain unchanged; L_token is renamed L_CEL. Section 6.3.4 adds an optional integration with Batch Prioritized Routing during inference. Bias-only gradient extraction is newly documented implementation information, without establishing a redesign of the method used for retained results.

E1.justification: Section 6.5 and Table 12 extend evaluation from vision-language tasks to text-only GLUE tasks: CoLA, MRPC, QNLI, MNLI and RTE. Existing visual benchmarks and the 665K/1021K training-data comparisons remain; the newly detailed training-mixture constituents do not establish additional coverage.

E2.justification: v3 Table 4 expands the earlier embedding-versus-gradient comparison with feature-based and task-based routing implementations within MoE-LLaVA, documented in Section 6.2. Table 10 also introduces comparisons with Batch Prioritized Routing enabled. The headline LVLM comparator set in Table 1 remains unchanged.

E3.justification: New evaluations introduce BERT-large with eight experts and Top-2 activation, inference-capacity tests at 2.0 and 0.5 with and without Batch Prioritized Routing, and additional gradient-diagnostic metrics and procedures. Newly disclosed training settings for retained experiments do not establish that those experiments were changed or rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds load-balancing-weight and loss-design ablations, capacity robustness tests, activated-pathway analysis, gradient distributions, feature-gradient correlations and confusing-token case studies. Threshold and regularizer-weight sweeps are retained. Conversely, v2 Table 4(a)'s layer-subset ablation and Figure 3(a)'s direct routing-score diagnostic are removed.

E5.justification: Section 6.3.3 and Figure 8 newly report standard deviation of gradient consistency across experts, extending v2's mean-based summaries. This measures across-expert dispersion, not repeated-run uncertainty. Neither version reports experimental seed counts, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Headline benchmark scores in Tables 1–2 and the relocated scalability results remain unchanged. The expanded embedding comparison replaces results, including GQA 56.1 in v2 Table 3(a) with 57.0 in v3 Table 4. New results include GLUE averages of 81.5 for reimplemented MoE and 82.8 with STGC, computational overhead, robustness and diagnostic findings; several older ablation entries disappear.

T1.justification: Beyond v2's conflicting-token definition and first-order interference argument, Section 6.6 introduces convexity and Lipschitz-gradient assumptions, a learning-rate restriction and a descent/convergence derivation around Equation 15. This substantially expands the theory, although its purported loss-increase case requires an unattainable cosine condition.

C1.justification: Both versions claim that token-gradient identification and a routing regularizer reduce expert interference, provide a plug-in for MoE-based LVLMs and improve performance, particularly with more diverse training data. Rewritten motivation and additional supporting experiments do not materially redefine these central contributions.

C2.justification: v3 adds the limitation that detecting conflict with a current expert does not identify the optimal alternative expert. It also explains the mean-gradient choice through training stability, discusses training overhead, interprets residual conflicts in shallow layers, and develops explanations involving routing pathways, loss optimization and feature-gradient relationships.

D1.justification: Sections 6.1–6.4 disclose bias-gradient extraction, cosine averaging, parameter freezing, training hyperparameters, hardware, precision, data-mixture prompts and comparator implementations. They explicitly identify the 1021K training setting behind Table 1 and report throughput and memory estimates. These substantially improve implementation documentation; the promised code-release location remains unchanged.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands positioning against recent MoE and LoRA approaches, including Octavius/LoRA-MoE, MoLA, MoME, CuMo and Uni-MoE. It adds distinctions from PCGrad and discussions of compatibility with V-MoE and MoNE. DEMIX and several broad LLM references disappear.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work and methodological explanations receive extensive rewriting around router optimization and conflicting-token identification. Ablation discussion is reordered, a limitations subsection is added, and a structured seven-part supplement is introduced. Terminology, author information and conference headers are also updated.

P2.justification: Figure 3 removes panels and rearranges retained curves; the threshold and loss-weight tables are consolidated, and the scalability table is relocated. Expert-loading displays are revised and expanded with routing pathways. Numerous new supplementary tables and plots present implementation settings, diagnostics, robustness, computational costs and language results.

improvement.justification: v2 leaves practical gradient extraction and training costs largely unexplained. v3 documents the bias-gradient approximation, training settings and approximately 21% step-time overhead, substantially improving reproducibility and feasibility assessment. New routing, loss and capacity controls plus language-task results strengthen validation. These gains outweigh removed diagnostics and introduced weaknesses: Section 6.6 uses an impossible cosine condition, and Table 4 reports a task-based average of 48.9 although its listed scores average about 55.0.
